Kewana and Adam are earning money by painting both sides of a fence. When it was lunch time, they decided to compare who has painted more since they started. Use the number line to find out which student has painted more of the fence.
Kewana has painted 2/3 of one side of the fence.
Adam has painted 4/7 of the other side of the fence.
Who has painted more fence?

hints.message: What does the denominator tell you about the number line?
Use the denominator of Kewana's fraction to decide how many equal intervals are needed from 0 to 1.
Look at the bottom number in Kewana's fraction and enter that number of equal parts.
Enter the number of equal intervals indicated by the denominator of 2/3.

misconceptions.description: Aluno confunde o número de marcas com o número de divisões (intervalos).
misconceptions.feedback: You counted the dividing marks instead of the intervals. To make 3 equal intervals, the number line must contain 3 spaces between 0 and 1.

hints.message: What does the numerator tell you about the intervals on the number line?
Starting at 0, count equal intervals toward 1 until you reach the number shown by the numerator.
Kewana's point is two equal intervals from 0, not at the halfway point.
Move to the second mark after 0 on the line divided into thirds.

misconceptions.description: Aluno usa a metade como referência para tudo.
misconceptions.feedback: You marked the halfway point. Kewana's fraction uses thirds, and two thirds is not exactly one half.

misconceptions.description: Aluno trata o numerador como uma posição absoluta na reta.
misconceptions.feedback: You used the numerator as a whole-number position. The line goes from 0 to 1, so 2/3 must be placed between 0 and 1.

nodes.description: Set the second number line to 7 equal parts for Adam's fraction.
nodes.instruction: Set the second number line to 7 equal parts for Adam's fraction.

hints.message: Which part of a fraction tells you how many equal sections to make?
Read the denominator in Adam's fraction and use it as the number of equal intervals.
Adam's denominator is larger than Kewana's denominator, so his line needs more equal intervals.
Enter the number of intervals named by the bottom number in 4/7.
How many equal intervals from 0 does Adam's numerator represent?
Start at 0 and count the equal seventh intervals toward 1.
Adam's point is four intervals from 0 on the line divided into sevenths.
Move to the fourth mark after 0 on the number line divided into sevenths.

nodes.description: Compare the two points and choose who painted more fence.

options.label: Adam painted more fence.
options.feedback: You focused on the fraction with the larger numerator and denominator. Compare the relative positions of 2/3 and 4/7 on the number lines.

Compare the locations of the two marked points between 0 and 1.
Focus on which painted amount is closer to 1 on its number line.
Choose the student whose marked point is farther to the right.
